newsitem.title: USA: Wal-Mart, TJX post robust earnings; J.C. Penney's fall.
newsitem.headline: Wal-Mart, TJX post robust earnings; J.C. Penney's fall.

text.p: Wal-Mart Stores Inc. and TJX Cos. Inc. reported Tuesday that earnings rose robustly in the second quarter, but J.C. Penney Co. Inc.'s profits fell after factoring in costs for acquiring Eckerd Drugstores.
Overall, the results showed retailers are reaping the benefits of lean inventories, which have helped lower costs and reduce the need for merchandise markdowns, analysts said.

"By and large the earnings today have been at least as good if not better than expected," said Michael Exstein of investment bank CS First Boston. "It's the first time in about four years that the industry has been in synch."

Wal-Mart, the nation's largest retailer, said earnings rose to $795 million, or 35 cents a share, during the second quarter from $706 million, or 31 cents a share, last year. Sales rose 11 percent to $28.4 billion from $25.6 billion in 1996.
The results were in line with Wall Street expectations, according to First Call Corp., which tracks analyst forecasts.
"All of our retail businesses experienced strong sales and significant improvements in operating income over the similar prior-year quarter," Wal-Mart President David Glass said in a statement.

It was the third straight quarter that Wal-Mart's earnings per share, which were up 13 percent, have grown more quickly than sales, showing tight inventory and expense control have fallen to the bottom line, analysts said.

Wal-Mart's international division swung to a profit from a loss last year on strength in the Mexican and Canadian markets and as stores turn profitable after covering initial start-up costs, analysts said.
Inventories at Wal-Mart's domestic stores fell by more than $300 million during the quarter, the company said.

Wal-Mart has been "very consistent in controlling the enterprise," said CS First Boston's Exstein. "They are flowing the inventories better to the stores. They don't have as many inventory markdowns."

At J.C. Penney, net income fell to $90 million, or 32 cents a share, during the second quarter from $93 million, or 37 cents a share, in the same period last year. The results included costs related to the purchase of Eckerd Corp. for $3.3 billion earlier this year.
Minus those expenses, Penney's operating earnings rose to 38 cents a share. The results exceeded analysts' estimates of 37 cents a share for the period.

Still, the period was not a spectacular one for Penney, whose 95-year-old department store business faltered while the company bulked up on drug stores. Department store sales, particularly of women's apparel, were disappointing, and inventories swelled last year and earlier this year after a switch to more-fashionable merchandise did not catch on.

On Monday, Penney offered early retirement to about 1,500 workers in an effort to thin its management ranks by 5 percent. The reduction was expected to result in a charge of $200 million this year and to trim expenses by 25 cents a share annually beginning next year.
"We have in place merchandising and marketing programmes to generate profitable sales for the all-important second half," Penney Chairman James Oesterreicher said in a statement issued Tuesday.
Inventories were up at the end of the second quarter but not as drastically as in the first quarter, and the number of promotional sales events was down, analysts said.

Off-price clothing retailer TJX Cos. said it earned $52.6 million, or 29 cents a share, during the second quarter, compared with $36.1 million, or 20 cents a share, in the same period in 1996. Sales rose 10 percent to $1.7 billion from $1.5 billion.
The results exceeded analysts' estimates of 26 cents a share. TJX has benefited from cost savings and buying power resulting from its acquisition of Marshalls from Melville Corp. in 1995.

"For this year's second quarter, as well as the first half, results are substantially ahead of what we anticipated," TJX President Bernard Cammarata said in a statement. "Both T.J. Maxx and Marshalls achieved strong year-over-year comparable store sales increases. Our success was broadly spread throughout our geographic regions and merchandise categories."

He said same-store sales, or sales at stores open at least a year, rose 8 percent during the quarter, which the company tied to its inventory management and the stocking of attractive merchandise in its stores.
Penney's stock jumped $2.50 to $60.625, TJX gained 75 cents to $29.50 and Wal-Mart was up 12.5 cents at $36.875, all in consolidated afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
